newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK residential property market in crisis - Salomon.
newsitem.headline: HK residential property market in crisis - Salomon.

text.p: Hong Kong's residential property market is in a crisis which could take three to five years to address, with supply well short of demand, prices high and speculation rife, Salomon Brothers said in a recent report.
"A cocktail of social frustration and an undermining of the pillars of Hong Kong's unique property-orientated economy are in the making," property analyst Michael Green said.
In the report, dated January 14, Green severely criticised the Hong Kong government for creating a land shortage problem.
"The major cause for the shortage is the ineptitude of government planning," he said.

"The supply shortage was worsened by the slow rate of Approval to Commence Work on projects. This, in turn was caused by a combination of increased bureaucracy and lack of understanding of the market," he added.
The report said a decline in Consents to Commence work in 1994 and 1995 had not only led to a decline in supply in 1996 but would also lead to a substantial shortage in 1998 and 1999.

A 30 percent downpayment requirement for mortgage loans "has contributed to speculation as a structural feature of the market," it added. If banks continue to lend the savings pool to speculators, prices would continue moving higher.
"To cap it all, Hong Kong is in the final stage of its transition from British colonial rule to Special Administrative Region status of the People's Republic of China," said Green.
Demand for housing and offices was likely to be increasingly difficult to forecast over coming years, since it was hard to assess the inflow of people from China to Hong Kong, he added.

"Immigration to Hong Kong by wealthy Chinese could push prices upward and out of reach of many Hong Kong people from time to time, while poorer immigrants from China could undercut wage levels of Hong Kong people and exacerbate tensions," the report said.
Salomon said a residential property strategy should be put in place which should include a provision for a permanent strategic land reserve.

"Speculation should not be legislated against, but rather controlled through ruthless resolve to tax those indulging in the legitimate commercial business of buying stock in trade and selling their merchandise like any other trader," he added.

Green also said it was "vitally important" to introduce a Mortage Corporation as soon as possible. "It is highly inadequate in an economy such as that of Hong Kong, which is highly geared to property, that such an organistion does not yet exist."
Banks provide the largest amount of finance for property loans and delays in establishing a Mortgage Corporation could result in a larger burden of financing directly from the banks, the report said.

"Regardless of whether or not the government puts together a comprehensive and credible strategy for the property market, it is likely that the residential market is going to be volatile over the next two to three years," the report said.

"To prevent excessive instability, it may be necessary for increased direct cooperation between the larger property developers, the larger banks and the government to closely coordinate the release of finance with the sale of developments and the seasonal factors which influence this market," the report said.
